## 1. The mini research project {#sec-4141-project-overview}

::: {.callout-note title="Why do we do a mini research project?"}
Lectures and textbooks can only take you so far. Doing research shows you things that are hard to appreciate any other way.

**You see how ideas become measurable.** From the inside, you see how researchers turn abstract ideas into measurable variables: how instructions are worded, questions are designed and responses are recorded. You may also notice how your own expectations shape what you do. These are the issues you’ll need to think critically about in your own designs, such as demand characteristics, operationalisation and measurement validity.

**You see ethics in practice.** Information sheets, informed consent, the right to withdraw and debriefing make more sense once you’ve implemented them.

**You see why sample size and representativeness matter.** Your own research will depend on others choosing to take part, and the project gives you a first-hand sense of that.

In short, the mini project helps you become a better researcher by connecting what you learn in class to real research practice.
:::

## 2. Key readings: Start with these papers to get a better understanding of the main concepts {#sec-4141-project-reading}

These papers are **essential reading** to get started on the research project. Focus on how concepts are defined, operationalised and measured. 

Smallwood, J., & Schooler, J. W. (2015). The science of mind wandering: Empirically navigating the stream of consciousness. *Annual Review of Psychology, 66*, 487–518. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010814-015331

Kaye, L. K., Orben, A., Ellis, D. A., Hunter, S. C., & Houghton, S. (2020). The conceptual and methodological mayhem of “screen time”. *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 17*(10), Article 3661. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17103661

Baumgartner, S. E., Parry, D. A., Beyens, I., Wiradhany, W., Uncapher, M., Wagner, A. D., & Bavelier, D. (2024). The short- and long-term effects of digital media use on attention. In D. A. Christakis & L. Hale (Eds.), *Handbook of children and screens: Digital media, development, and well-being from birth through adolescence* (pp. 31-37). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-69362-5_5

:::{.callout-tip}
All reading is accessible via the library. You can go to Moodle -> Library Resources -> Resource List or you can follow [**this link**](https://eu.alma.exlibrisgroup.com/leganto/public/44LAN_INST/lists/93496942590001221?auth=SAML&section=94028195020001221).
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="Next steps"}
Once you have gained a foundational understanding of the key concepts mind wandering and screen time from reading the papers mentioned above, search the literature for studies investigating an association between the two. Look for studies that measure the aspects you find most interesting and see what they found. Are the results consistent across studies? If not, what might explain inconsistencies? What do you think is the next step that follows logically from the study or studies that you found? 
:::

## 3. How to write a good research question ... and appropriate hypotheses?{#sec-4141-project-research-question}

:::{.callout-important title=}
Each group will investigate the broad question *Is mind wandering associated with screen time*.

With your group you need to:

1. Refine the research topic to hone in on specific aspects of the key concepts of mind wandering and screen time.
2. Formulate a clear and specific research question.
3. Write a null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis.
:::

## 4. Measuring mind wandering and screen time {#sec-4141-project-measures}

:::{.callout-important}
With your group you need to decide how to measure the variables you've specified in your research question. In this module we focus on using questionnaires to measure constructs.

The questionnaire needs to be:

1. open access (that is, openly available and free to use);
2. accompanied by a peer-reviewed article that discusses the construction, validity and reliability of the questionnaire.

Below I've listed some examples, but you can propose a different questionnaire you have found in the literature as long as it satisfies the above criteria. Asking people to report (a specific aspect of) their screen-time as recorded in a screentime app is also acceptable.
:::

:::{.callout-tip}
Fife-Schaw, C. (2020). 14: Questionnaire design. In G. M. Breakwell, D. B. Wright, & J. Barnett (Eds.), Research methods in psychology (5th ed., pp. 119–138). SAGE Publications. **Recommended**

> This chapter provides a useful overview of things to consider when setting up a questionnaire study.
:::

:::{.callout-tip}
All reading is accessible via the library. You can go to Moodle -\> Library Resources -\> Resource List or you can follow [**this link**](https://lancaster.alma.exlibrisgroup.com/leganto/nui/lists/93496942590001221).
:::

**Examples of papers that discuss questionnaires that measure mind wandering**

Carriere, J. S. A., Seli, P., & Smilek, D. (2013). Wandering in both mind and body: Individual differences in mind wandering and inattention predict fidgeting. *Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology/Revue canadienne de psychologie expérimentale, 67*(1), 19–31. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031438

> Carriere et al. (2013) capture two forms of mind wandering using the Mind Wandering: Spontaneous (MW-S) and Mind Wandering: Deliberate (MW-D) scales.

Mrazek, M. D., Phillips, D. T., Franklin, M. S., Broadway, J. M., & Schooler, J. W. (2013). Young and restless: Validation of the Mind-Wandering Questionnaire (MWQ) reveals disruptive impact of mind-wandering for youth. *Frontiers in Psychology, 4*, Article 560. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00560

> Mrazek et al. (2013) created a 5-item Mind-Wandering Questionnaire (MWQ) and showed across four studies that people who score higher on it report more task-unrelated thoughts during a reading test.

Schubert, A.-L., Frischkorn, G. T., Sadus, K., Welhaf, M. S., Kane, M. J., & Rummel, J. (2024). The brief mind wandering three-factor scale (BMW-3). *Behavior Research Methods, 56*(8), 8720–8744. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-024-02500-6

> During the first weeks of term, during the lab session you worked with some publicly available data from a research project on mind wandering carried out by Schubert and colleagues (Schubert et al., 2024). They created a 12-item questionnaire that measures how often your mind wanders without meaning to, how often you let it wander on purpose, and how aware you are when it happens.

**Examples of papers on measuring aspects of screen time**

In addition to the paper by Kaye et al. (2020) referred to in the section with key readings (@sec-4141-project-reading), the following papers are good examples of papers that focus on a specific aspect of screen time. 

Baumgartner, S. E., Lemmens, J. S., Weeda, W. D., & Huizinga, M. (2017). Measuring media multitasking: Development of a short measure of media multitasking for adolescents. *Journal of Media Psychology, 29*(4), 188–197. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-1105/a000167

> Baumgartner et al. (2017) developed a short media multitasking measure (MMM-S) -- measuring the simultaneous use of two or more media. 

Du, J., van Koningsbruggen, G. M., & Kerkhof, P. (2018). A brief measure of social media self-control failure. *Computers in Human Behavior, 84*, 68–75. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2018.02.002

> Du et al. (2018) developed a 3-item scale, the Social Media Self-Control Failure (SMSCF) scale, to measure how often people give in to social media temptations. 

Marty-Dugas, J., Ralph, B. C., Oakman, J. M., & Smilek, D. (2018). The relation between smartphone use and everyday inattention. *Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice, 5*(1), 46. https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/cns0000131

> Marty-Dugas et al. (2018) developed two different measures of smartphone use (general and absent-minded) and explore relationships with measures of everyday inattention.

Ohme, J., Araujo, T., de Vreese, C. H., & Piotrowski, J. T. (2021). Mobile data donations: Assessing self-report accuracy and sample biases with the iOS Screen Time function. *Mobile Media & Communication, 9*(2), 293-313. https://doi.org/10.1177/2050157920959106

> Ohme et al. (2021) present a new methodological approach: mobile data donations using screenshots of the iOS Screen Time function. They assesses its feasibility, sample biases, and the accuracy of self-reported smartphone usage compared to log data in a general population sample of Dutch citizens.

## 5. Pre-register your research question, hypotheses and measures and using the feedback {#sec-4141-preregistration}

:::{.callout-tip title="Why pre-register?"}

Pre-registration means writing down your research question, hypotheses and measures *before* you collect any data. It is increasingly common in psychology because it:

- makes you commit to a clear plan, so you can tell the difference between what you predicted and what you discovered along the way
- guards against changing your hypotheses or analyses after seeing the results, which can make findings look stronger than they are
- makes your reasoning transparent, so others can see what you set out to do and why
- gives you a chance to get feedback on your plan while you can still change it

Here, it also means that you have settled the key decisions for your study before you start building it.
:::

### What your group needs to do

Each group needs to:

- Refine the research topic to focus on specific aspects of the key concepts of mind wandering and screen time.
- Formulate a clear and specific research question.
- Write a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis.
- Specify how you are proposing to measure the key constructs.

More information on how to do this, and suggested papers about questionnaires you could use, can be found in the sections [How to write a good research question ... and appropriate hypotheses?](@sec-4141-project-research-question) and [Measuring mind wandering and screen time](@sec-4141-project-measures).

Once you have made these decisions as a group, one of you needs to complete the pre-registration form. **Please check the Moodle announcement for the link to the form and the deadline.**

### Feedback on your pre-registrations

Thank you for submitting your pre-registrations. The module coordinator has read through your pre-registrations and given each group individual feedback. Many of you made a good start, and the same issues came up often enough that I have collected them into an overview of common issues, with do's and don'ts, that you can check your own project against. Nearly all of them come back to one idea: your research question, definitions, measures and hypotheses need to describe the same thing, that is they need to align.

#### Keep a golden thread: question, concept, measure, hypothesis
The most common issue was a mismatch between what the research question says you are studying and what your questionnaire or measure actually captures. Before you finalise anything, check each link in the chain:

- Does the research question name the specific constructs you are measuring, in the same terms that the questionnaires use?
- Does each measure capture the construct as you have defined it, not a related one?
- Do the hypotheses follow directly from the research question and refer to the same variables?

::: {.callout-tip}
If you change one part (for example, you switch your screen time measure), you will usually need to reformulate the research question and the hypotheses to match.
:::

#### Measure mind wandering, not related concepts
The assignment is to investigate (an aspect of) mind wandering. Several research questions and answers to 'What aspect of mind wandering are you proposing to investigate?' referred to concepts that are related to mind wandering but are not the same thing, such as:

- attention span, sustained attention, lack of focus, poor attentional control
- distracted behaviour, phone checking
- daydreaming
- information retention, quality or amount of notes, work output, effort

In everyday language these may sound similar, but in the scientific literature they are separate constructs. Some of them (like notes or work output) are likely *consequences* of mind wandering rather than mind wandering itself. Keep this in mind when you describe findings from the literature in your report: make sure the studies you cite actually looked at mind wandering. Smallwood and Schooler (2015) explain how mind wandering is defined and measured, so re-read it if you are unsure.

::: {.callout-tip title="Easy access to readings"}
All reading is accessible via the library. You can go to Moodle -\>
Library Resources -\> Resource List or you can follow [**this
link**](https://lancaster.alma.exlibrisgroup.com/leganto/nui/lists/93496942590001221).
:::

#### Be specific about which type of mind wandering
The questionnaires differ in what they measure:

- Mrazek et al. (2013) measures mind wandering in general. It does not distinguish intentional/deliberate from unintentional/spontaneous mind wandering.
- Carriere et al. (2013) measures spontaneous and deliberate mind wandering. These terms are used interchangeably in the literature with unintentional and intentional, but it is neater to use the terms from your questionnaire in your research question, hypotheses and report.
- Schubert et al. (2024) measures intentional mind wandering, unintentional mind wandering and meta-awareness of mind wandering.

What this means for you:

- If your research question says 'mind wandering', that is fine only if you are measuring mind wandering in general. If you want to focus on one type, say so in the research question and choose a questionnaire that can measure it.
- If you use all three aspects of the Schubert questionnaire, think about whether you expect the same or a different relationship between screen time and each aspect, and write your hypotheses accordingly. You may also choose to use only the questions for one or two aspects.
- Use the questionnaire items exactly as written. Changing the items would invalidate the questionnaire and make it difficult to compare your results with other studies.

#### If you study mind wandering in a specific context, adapt the instructions carefully
Many groups added a context to the research question (during lectures, independent study, academic settings, the morning). That is a good way to make a question more specific, but the questionnaires are written to ask about everyday mind wandering, so you have to deal with that. The simplest option is to use the questionnaire developed by Carriere et al. (as the phrasing of their questions still make sense if you change the context) and make a small change to the instruction that participants see, not to the items themselves. Specifically, Carriere et al. ask participants to reflect on their 'everyday mind wandering'; you could instead ask about mind wandering 'while attending university lectures'. If you do this:

- Define the context for participants (for example, are in-person and pre-recorded lectures included? What counts as independent study or an academic session?). Give examples.
- Make sure the questions still make sense in that context.
- Justify in your report why you chose the context and describe how you adapted the instruction.

The same logic applies to screen time: if you are interested in a particular time of day (such as the morning scroll), you can build that into the instruction.

#### Decide how you will measure screen time, and make sure it matches your question

This was the second most common issue, and we recognise this may have partly come about by the way the module coordinator phrased parts of the pre-registration form. Many groups described screen time as a specific behaviour (for example, time spent on TikTok or time watching short-form content) but selected a questionnaire that measures something different:

- Baumgartner et al. (2017) measures media multitasking; 
- Du et al. (2018) measures social media self-control failure;
-	Marty-Dugas et al. (2018) measures general and absent-minded smartphone use.

These are all related to screen time, but none of them is the same as the amount of time people spend on an app or a type of content. Please decide which of the following you will do, and make your research question and hypotheses fit that decision:

- Ask participants to log their time on particular apps (a direct but self-reported measure of time spent).
- Use a questionnaire (which measures a particular behaviour or experience linked to screen time, not time spent).
- Use both. This is allowed, but you must explain why in your introduction, and consider whether you expect the same or different associations with mind wandering for each measure.

If you ask participants to log their usage:
- Ask for minutes, not hours. 125 minutes is easier to work with than '2 hours and 5 minutes'.
- Give clear instructions on where to find the information on their phone, which apps to include and over which period (for example, yesterday or the past week).
- Define the category you are asking about. What counts as social media or short-form content? Does anything you can send messages on count?
- Keep it as a continuous variable. You don't need to split people into high and low users as we are using a correlational design (not a group comparison design)
- We can check whether it is possible on Gorilla to ask participants to upload a screenshot as a check, in addition to the logged minutes.

#### Hypotheses: correlational wording, correct logic
Our design is correlational, so the wording of your hypotheses has to reflect that.

**Do{style="color: green;"}:**

-	State the null hypothesis as: there is no association (correlation) between X and Y.
-	State the alternative hypothesis as: there is an association between X and Y (non-directional), or there is a positive (as X goes up, Y goes up) or negative (as X goes up, Y goes down) association (directional).
-	Be specific if you have several measures or aspects of mind wandering: say what you expect for each.
-	In your report, justify whether your hypothesis is directional or non-directional using studies from the literature.

**Don't{style="color: red;"}:**

-	Use causal language such as 'effect on', ' more of X increases Y', 'more of X leads to' or 'X causes Y'. With a correlational design, we cannot know whether X causes Y, Y causes X, or something else drives both.
-	Swap the null and alternative hypotheses. The null states there is no association.
-	Frame the question as a group comparison (for example, more or less than 4 hours). We are using correlation, so keep screen time continuous.
-	Add things that don't come out of your measures (such as a score out of 10).

#### Keep the scope manageable
Some research questions contained several questions in one (for example, social media use and attention, social media use and information retention, and an age comparison). Choose one relationship and one population. When you choose a population, check your hidden assumptions (for example, do people in this group use the platform you are asking about?) and think about how you will recruit them.

::: {.callout-tip title="Quick checklist"}
Use the checklist below to check your project:

- [ ] My research question names the specific constructs I am measuring, not broader or related ones.
- [ ] My definition of mind wandering and my questionnaire match.
- [ ] My screen time measure matches how I describe screen time in the research question.
- [ ] If I adapted instructions for a context, I have defined the context and can justify the choice.
- [ ] My hypotheses use correlational language, have the null and alternative the right way round, and fit my measures.
- [ ] My question is small enough to answer with one correlational design.
:::

:::{.callout-important title="How to use the feedback"}
You can use this feedback in two ways:

1. **To build your study on Gorilla.** The feedback helps you check that the measures you build are the ones you decided on, and what you need to know before you start. Please refer to the section on [**Building your study on Gorilla**](@sec-4141-project-building) for step by step guidance.
2. **To write the introduction for your research report.** The same decisions shape the introduction of your research report, which needs to make an argument for why your study makes sense and why it is designed the way it is. Please refer to the section on [**Building the rationale for your study**](@sec-4141-project-rationale) to help you plan this.
:::

## 7. Building your study on Gorilla {#sec-4141-project-building}

### Getting set up:

To build your group's questionnaire study on Gorilla, each group needs to clone an example project and then amend that project. The example project contains the following components:

- Participant information sheet
- Consent form
- Debrief sheet

#### What you need to do as a group:

1. One member of your group needs to sign in to Gorilla and carry out assignment 1: Clone the example project and add collaborators. Information on how to clone a project is [here](https://support.gorilla.sc/support/publishing-and-open-science/sharing#cloningaproject).

2. That same group member then needs to add the other group members as collaborators. Information on how to add collaborators is [here](https://support.gorilla.sc/support/publishing-and-open-science/sharing#collaborating).

### Preparing your study for Gorilla

Now that you have made your key decisions, the next step is to build your study on Gorilla. Before you open Gorilla, work through the **Preparing your study for Gorilla** activity as a group. It takes about an hour and helps you check that what you build matches what you decided to measure, and that you have all the information you need to build it.

By the end, your group will have a build sheet for three questionnaires:

- **Mind wandering**
- **Screen time**
- **Demographics**, adapted to the people you are recruiting

The activity has four steps:

1. **Write down what you decided.** Summarise your research question, population, measures and hypotheses, and check that they all describe the same thing.
2. **Complete a build sheet for each measure.** For each questionnaire, work out the information you need before building it, such as the exact items, instructions, response scales and scoring.
3. **Plan your data.** List the variables you will collect and decide the order in which participants see the questionnaires.
4. **Build, check and test.** Build the questionnaires in your cloned Gorilla project, check that you are using the correct participant information sheet, consent form and debrief sheet, and test everything before you recruit anyone.

The [Preparing your study for Gorilla document](files/project/preparing_your_study_for_Gorilla.docx) has the full instructions, worked examples, and boxes for your group to fill in. Download it and complete it as a group before you start building.

### Building your own measures

Once you all have a Gorilla account, have cloned the example project and have added all group memebers as collaborators, you are ready to start adding your own measures to measure demographics, mind wandering and screen time.

::: {.callout-tip}
Guidance on how to do that can be found in the section above on **Learning about the Gorilla platform** [here](@sec-4141-project-gorilla).

The [Gorilla reference guide on how to use their Questionnaire builder](https://support.gorilla.sc/support/tools/questionnaire-builder-2) is also useful.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Checklist: Before you build the individual measures"}
Check that everything below is in place before you start building your three questionnaires in Gorilla.

**Your decisions**

- [ ] My research question, definitions, measures and hypotheses all describe the same thing.
- [ ] I know who we are recruiting, including the age range and any other criteria for taking part.

**Mind wandering questionnaire**

- [ ] We know which questionnaire and which aspect of mind wandering we are measuring.
- [ ] We have the exact wording of every item, copied from the paper.
- [ ] We have the instruction wording, including any adaptation for a context, and have defined the context.
- [ ] We have the response scale and labels, exactly as published.
- [ ] We know how the score is calculated, including any reverse-scored items.

**Screen time measure**

- [ ] We have decided whether to use a usage log, a questionnaire or both.
- [ ] We have defined exactly what counts as screen time, and which time period we are asking about.
- [ ] We have written the exact question wording, and clear instructions for where participants find the information.
- [ ] We have decided the unit and format of the answer (for example, minutes as a whole number).

**Demographics questionnaire**

- [ ] The questions fit the people we are recruiting. If we specified an age range, we ask for age.
- [ ] Every question is needed for checking eligibility or describing our sample.
- [ ] We have decided what happens to participants who do not meet our criteria.

**Data**

- [ ] We have a list of the variables we will collect, how each is calculated, and what we will name each one.
- [ ] Everyone in the group agrees on the plan, and we have completed the build sheet from the *Preparing your study for Gorilla* activity.

**You can download [this checklist](files/project/checklist_1_before_building_the_measures.docx) as a Word document and use it with your group if you like.**
:::

:::{.callout-important}
Gorilla uses **Version control**. This means that it keeps a record of all the saved changes to the project. Whenever you have finished editing a component, you will need to commit the changes before a different group member can access that specific component. Have a look at [this page](https://support.gorilla.sc/support/tools/questionnaire-builder-2/step-by-step#commit) for a more detailed explanation. It will ask you to add a 'Commit message'. This is a short description of the changes that you implemented that time. So you'd write something like: Added questions 1 to 4'. Keep it short, but make sure to write an informative message. This will make it easier to go back to a previous version if something goes wrong.
:::

### Building your Experiment

Once all the individual components are in place, build your experiment. Use the checklist below to check that you are ready to start building:

::: {.callout-tip}
Gorilla's Experiment Builder support pages [here](https://support.gorilla.sc/support/tools/experiment-builder) provide guidance.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Checklist: Before you put your study together in the Experiment Builder"}
Check that everything below is in place before you start assembling your study in Gorilla's Experiment Builder.

**Your questionnaires**

- [ ] All three questionnaires (mind wandering, screen time and demographics) are built.
- [ ] We have checked every item, instruction and scale label against our build sheet.
- [ ] We have tried each questionnaire as a participant, including answers that should not work, such as leaving a question blank or typing letters in a number box.
- [ ] We have looked at each questionnaire on a phone and on a laptop.

**Participant materials**

- [ ] We have cloned the project that contains the participant information sheet, consent form and debrief sheet, and we are working inside that clone.
- [ ] I have read the participant information sheet, consent form and debrief sheet, and they are the correct versions for this study.

**Order**

- [ ] We have decided the order of the three questionnaires, and why.
- [ ] The information sheet and consent form will come first, before any questionnaire, and the debrief sheet will come last.

**You can download [this checklist](files/project/checklist_2_before_the_experiment_builder.docx) as a Word document and use it with your group if you like.**
:::

:::{.callout-tip}
You can meet up as a group and work on it together, or you can assign individual group members who will work on different parts.
:::

:::{.callout-important}
Gorilla uses **Version control**. This means that it keeps a record of all the saved changes to the project. Whenever you have finished editing a component, you will need to commit the changes before a different group member can access that specific component. Have a look at [this page](https://support.gorilla.sc/support/tools/questionnaire-builder-2/step-by-step#commit) for a more detailed explanation. It will ask you to add a 'Commit message'. This is a short description of the changes that you implemented that time. So you'd write something like: Added questions 1 to 4'. Keep it short, but make sure to write an informative message. This will make it easier to go back to a previous version if something goes wrong.
:::
